description: Successive waves of arrival — Irish dockers, Jewish refugees from Tsarist Russia and Bangladeshi migrants.
content_html:
Irish Migration to Spitalfields

The Huguenot community’s prosperity gradually declined after the 1770s, as the silk trade faced competition and the Spitalfields Act was eventually repealed. Irish Catholics began settling in Spitalfields and the surrounding Whitechapel area from the late eighteenth century, with larger waves following the Irish Famine (1845–1852). Irish migrants worked as dock labourers, street sellers and in casual labouring trades. They concentrated in the cheapest, most overcrowded parts of Spitalfields, including the courts and alleys off Brick Lane. Their reception was often hostile — anti-Irish and anti-Catholic prejudice was widespread in Victorian England, and Irish workers faced competition with English labourers for scarce casual work in the East End docks.

Key Fact

Irish migrants in Spitalfields: settled from late 18th century, larger waves after the Famine (1845–52). Worked in docks, casual labour, street selling. Faced anti-Irish/anti-Catholic prejudice. Lived in the most overcrowded, poorest courts and alleys. Their experience contrasts with the Huguenots’ relatively skilled and prosperous arrival.

Jewish Migration: Fleeing the Pogroms

The largest single wave of migration to Spitalfields before the twentieth century was the arrival of Eastern European Jewish refugees from the 1880s onwards. Pogroms — organised massacres of Jewish communities — swept through the Russian Empire after 1881. Around 120,000 Jewish migrants arrived in Britain between 1880 and 1914, many settling in Spitalfields and Whitechapel. They worked in the garment trade, furniture-making, cabinet-making and as market traders in Petticoat Lane (Middlesex Street) and Brick Lane markets.

Jewish settlement transformed Spitalfields: Yiddish became the language of the streets, Jewish schools, synagogues and social clubs opened, and Jewish-owned businesses lined Brick Lane. The Huguenot chapel on Brick Lane had already become a Methodist chapel; around 1897 it was converted into the Great Synagogue (the building now known as Brick Lane Jamme Masjid). This conversion — a Huguenot chapel becoming a Jewish synagogue — shows the physical layering of migrant communities in a single building. Jewish migrants also faced hostility: the Aliens Act 1905 was partly a response to anti-Jewish feeling and marked the first major restriction on immigration to Britain.

The Battle of Cable Street (4 October 1936) was one of the most significant events in Spitalfields’ history. Sir Oswald Mosley’s British Union of Fascists planned to march through the Jewish East End. Around 100,000 anti-fascist demonstrators — Jewish, Irish, trade unionists and local residents — blocked the route at Cable Street. Mosley’s march was turned back. The battle demonstrated the solidarity of different working-class communities in Spitalfields against fascism, and remains a symbol of resistance in the area’s history.

Bangladeshi Settlement

Bangladeshi migrants began arriving in Spitalfields in significant numbers from the 1960s and 1970s, following earlier Sylheti sailors who had settled in the area. They worked in the garment trade — echoing the Huguenot weavers three centuries earlier — and opened restaurants on Brick Lane, which became famous as “Banglatown” by the 1980s and 1990s. In 1976, the Brick Lane synagogue was converted into a mosque — the Jamme Masjid — reflecting the new community’s dominance of the street.

Key Fact

Spitalfields migrant succession: Huguenots (from 1685) — Irish (from late 18th century, larger waves 1840s–50s) — Eastern European Jews (1880s–1914) — Bangladeshis (1960s–70s). Each wave settled in the same streets, often the same buildings, and faced a mixed reception from those already established.

Altab Ali, a 25-year-old Bangladeshi textile worker, was murdered in a racist attack in Whitechapel on 4 May 1978. His murder sparked the largest mobilisation of the Bangladeshi community in Britain up to that point: 7,000 people marched through the East End to Downing Street to demand protection. A park near the original attack site was renamed Altab Ali Park. His case shows that the Bangladeshi community in Spitalfields faced serious racist violence in the 1970s, and that their response was organised, political and assertive.

Patterns Across the Migrations

Looking across the four main waves of migration to Spitalfields, several patterns emerge. Each group arrived in response to persecution or economic necessity: Huguenots fled religious violence; the Irish fled famine and colonial poverty; Eastern European Jews fled pogroms; Bangladeshis migrated in search of economic opportunity and as part of post-war Commonwealth migration. Each group settled initially in the cheapest, most overcrowded parts of the area, then gradually built community institutions — churches, synagogues, mosques, community centres — that marked their permanent presence.

Reception by the host community varied but was rarely wholly welcoming. Anti-French feeling was common in the 1680s. Anti-Irish and anti-Catholic prejudice was documented throughout the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Anti-Jewish sentiment was embedded in legislation (Aliens Act 1905) as well as in street violence. Bangladeshi settlers faced both racist violence (the murder of Altab Ali, 1978) and organised fascist threats (the National Front’s activities in the 1970s and early 1980s). Yet all four communities established themselves, built lasting institutions, and contributed to the economic and cultural life of Spitalfields. This pattern of arrival, hostility, institution-building and gradual integration is the defining narrative of Spitalfields as a historic environment.
exam_tip_html: For the 10-mark historic environment source comparison, you must compare two sources about Spitalfields and use your own contextual knowledge to evaluate them. Make sure you integrate specific details about the successive migrant communities: the Huguenot–Jewish building sequence on Brick Lane, the Battle of Cable Street, the murder of Altab Ali. Comparisons that merely describe each source separately will not reach the highest marks — you need to show how the sources agree, differ, and what each reveals or conceals about migration in Spitalfields.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Spitalfields received four main migrant waves: Huguenots (1685+), Irish (late 18th century, especially post-Famine 1845–52), Eastern European Jews (1880s–1914), and Bangladeshis (1960s+); each settled in the same streets and often the same buildings, creating a layered history visible in the physical fabric of the area.
  • The Battle of Cable Street (4 October 1936) saw around 100,000 anti-fascists block Mosley’s march; the Brick Lane Jamme Masjid building’s conversion from synagogue to mosque in 1976 marked the shift to Bangladeshi community dominance of the street.
  • The murder of Altab Ali (1978) and the 7,000-strong march that followed it show that Bangladeshi settlers faced racist violence, but also organised politically to demand protection — a pattern of both hostility and community resistance that echoes earlier migrant experiences in the area.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Jewish community's settlement in Spitalfields after the 1880s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Precise feature with accurate detail (e.g. around 120,000 Jewish migrants arrived in Britain between 1880 and 1914, many working in the garment trade in Spitalfields and converting the Huguenot chapel on Brick Lane into a synagogue around 1897). Secure: Correct feature with some supporting information. Developing: Vague reference without specific detail. Emerging: Incorrect or irrelevant response.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Battle of Cable Street (1936).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two precise features (e.g. around 100,000 anti-fascists blocked Mosley's British Union of Fascists; the demonstrators included Jewish, Irish and trade union groups) each with accurate detail. Secure: Two features, at least one with detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate response.

practice_questions.text: Using your knowledge of Spitalfields, explain how the physical fabric of the area provides evidence for successive waves of migration.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Detailed explanation naming specific buildings (Brick Lane Jamme Masjid, Christ Church, Fournier Street terraces) and linking them to specific communities, showing how physical changes reveal migration history. Secure: Two or three specific examples with explanation. Developing: General reference to buildings without specific details. Emerging: Vague or incorrect response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why successive migrant communities in Spitalfields faced hostile reception from the settled population.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation covering economic competition (Irish dock labourers vs. English workers; garment trade), religious and racial prejudice (anti-Catholic, anti-semitism, racism against Bangladeshis), legal measures (Aliens Act 1905), and the specific experience of each community, with precise evidence. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence; at least two communities' experiences covered. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the Battle of Cable Street (1936) for the Spitalfields community? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument evaluating immediate significance (Mosley turned back, community solidarity demonstrated) and long-term impact (symbol of anti-fascist resistance, community identity), with counter-argument (e.g. fascist violence continued, limits of one event's impact). Secure: Clear argument with evidence across more than one dimension. Developing: Some argument; may focus on only one aspect. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Bangladeshi community's settlement in Spitalfields.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two precise features (e.g. worked in garment trade echoing Huguenot weavers; converted the Brick Lane synagogue into a mosque in 1976) each with accurate detail. Secure: Two features, at least one with detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate response.

flashcard_questions.a: Pogroms (organised massacres) in the Russian Empire after 1881

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Aliens Act (1905) partly a response to?
flashcard_questions.a: Anti-Jewish sentiment and pressure to restrict Eastern European Jewish immigration

flashcard_questions.q: What occupation linked Bangladeshi settlers to the original Huguenot settlers?
flashcard_questions.a: The garment/textile trade — both communities worked in textile production in Spitalfields

flashcard_questions.q: List the four migrant communities of Spitalfields in chronological order.
flashcard_questions.a: Huguenots (1685+), Irish (late 18th c.+), Eastern European Jews (1880s+), Bangladeshis (1960s+)

glossary_terms.definition: Jewish people who fled violent anti-Jewish persecution (pogroms) in the Russian Empire and Eastern Europe from the 1880s, settling in large numbers in the East End of London.
The Aliens Act 1905, partly passed in response to Jewish immigration, which gave the government power to refuse entry to immigrants deemed 'undesirable'.

The confrontation on 4 October 1936 in Cable Street, Whitechapel, when around 100,000 anti-fascist demonstrators (Jewish, Irish, labour movement) blocked Oswald Mosley's British Union of Fascists from marching through the Jewish East End.
People who migrated from what is now Bangladesh (then East Pakistan, then East Bengal) to Spitalfields and Tower Hamlets from the 1960s onwards, working mainly in the garment trade and restaurants.
Bangladeshi textile worker murdered in a racist attack in Whitechapel in 1978, whose death became a rallying point for the Bangladeshi community's campaign against racist violence.
